The decision settles the bigger of two legal fights over who governs one of Latin America’s most important new trade gateways. It tilts firmly toward the state.

For a reader abroad, the case turns on a deceptively simple question. Who makes the rules when private foreign money builds infrastructure that the public relies on?

What the Chancay port ruling decided

Lima’s Second Constitutional Chamber overturned a January decision by a lower court. That earlier ruling had ordered the transport regulator, known as Ositrán, to refrain from supervising the terminal.

The higher court threw out the challenge brought by the operator, Cosco Shipping. It found the company had shown no real threat to its rights that would justify blocking the regulator.

The heart of the reasoning is a category. Because the port is used by the public, the court held, the company running it counts as a service provider and falls under the regulator’s authority.

Crucially, that holds even though Chancay was built entirely with private money and without a state concession. Public use, not ownership, is what triggers oversight.

Why this fight matters more than the last one

An earlier ruling had already handed the state a narrow win on pricing at the port. But this case is broader and weightier.

The earlier decision covered only the regulator’s power to review tariffs. This one settles its full authority to regulate, supervise, inspect and penalise how the terminal operates day to day.

Cosco had argued the opposite with force. It said a privately financed port granted no state concession should sit outside the regulator’s reach, except on tariffs in narrow circumstances.

The court disagreed on the principle itself. That makes the ruling a precedent for every privately built asset that serves the public, well beyond this one terminal.

The geopolitics behind the docket

Chancay is no ordinary terminal. The roughly one-and-a-third-billion-dollar deep-water port opened in late 2024 and can take some of the largest ships afloat, cutting sailing time to Asia to around twenty-three days.

It is majority-owned by a Chinese state shipping group, which is why Washington watches it closely. US lawmakers have warned that the port could serve Chinese spying or future military use, claims Beijing rejects.

The ruling was the second legal blow to Cosco in a week. Days earlier, a court in Chancay upheld a market investigation by the competition agency, rejecting another company challenge.

The forward signal sits with the next government. Peru elects a new president who takes office in late July, and how firmly the state now asserts control at Chancay will test where the country leans between Beijing and Washington.

For investors, the ruling cuts two ways. It removes a cloud over how Chancay will be governed, which brings clarity, yet it also confirms that private builders here cannot escape the state’s reach.

Cosco can still fight specific decisions later. The court left open the ordinary administrative route to challenge any single regulatory act it believes oversteps, once such an act actually exists.

What it lost is the attempt to shut the regulator out in advance. That pre-emptive shield is gone, and the state now sits inside the port’s affairs rather than outside them.

What did the Chancay port ruling say?

A Lima appeals court gave Peru’s transport regulator, Ositrán, full authority to regulate and supervise the Chancay port, overturning a January decision that had ordered it to stand back. It threw out the legal challenge brought by the Chinese operator Cosco Shipping.

Why is the state allowed to regulate a private port?

The court held that because the port is used by the public, the company running it counts as a service provider subject to state oversight. Public use, rather than ownership, is what triggers regulation, even without a concession.

Why does the Chancay port matter globally?

Chancay is a deep-water hub that reroutes South American trade toward Asia and is majority-owned by a Chinese state group. That has made it a focus of the wider contest between China and the United States in Latin America.

Ebola deaths in DR Congo have passed 400, with 1,406 confirmed cases of the Bundibugyo strain and nearly a third of those infected dying. The outbreak is one of several crises across Africa today, from anti-migrant unrest in South Africa that has sent thousands fleeing to deadly floods in Ghana and Morocco’s football triumph over the Netherlands.

The continent is leaning on prayer, family support and football to carry on through grief over Ghana’s floods, anger over South Africa’s returning minister and the strain on ties with Nigeria.

South Africa – A Disgraced Minister Returns

An unwelcome comeback

President Cyril Ramaphosa reshuffled his cabinet late at night, appointing Dina Pule as social development minister, the same figure fired back in 2013 for unethical conduct.

Her new department oversees the social grants — regular government cash payments — that support tens of millions of the poorest South Africans.

A chorus of anger

Opposition parties, trade unions and anti-corruption groups all condemned the move, calling it a betrayal of public trust.

Pule now manages a budget of around 300 billion rand covering about 28 million people, making the outrage feel especially personal.

South Africa – Thousands Flee Anti-Migrant Unrest

Protests turn to looting

More than 900 people were arrested during Tuesday’s nationwide anti-migrant protests, which were mostly peaceful but marred by looting.

Of the 120 marches held, 108 stayed calm, yet the fear they spread has been enough to send families running.

Blame and displacement

Over 7,000 undocumented Malawians were sent home as a shelter in Pietermaritzburg closed its doors.

The rights group Amnesty argued that migrants are being unfairly blamed for problems rooted in the legacy of apartheid, the old system of racial separation.

Pule’s return after her 2013 dismissal felt to many South Africans like a slap in the face.

Nigeria – Abuja Demands Compensation

Counting the losses

Nigeria says it will seek compensation for citizens who abandoned homes and businesses while fleeing South Africa’s protests.

Officials are now documenting the losses of nationals who have returned home shaken and empty-handed.

A test between big economies

More than 600 Nigerians have already been evacuated, and Abuja disputes claims that all of them were living there illegally.

The dispute pits Africa’s two largest economies against each other and could sour relations for months.

DR Congo – Ebola Deaths Pass 400

A deadly climb

The health ministry says Ebola deaths have climbed above 400 after nearly 40 people died in a single day.

Confirmed cases have reached 1,406 of the Bundibugyo strain, with almost a third of those infected dying.

Fear meets resistance

Violence broke out in the town of Nia-Nia when residents refused to hand over a suspected Ebola body, and two people including a police officer were killed.

President Félix Tshisekedi has announced a 319 million dollar response plan, backed by donor pledges of 910 million dollars.

Ghana – Prayers After Deadly Floods

A nation on its knees

President John Dramani Mahama led a National Day of Prayer and Thanksgiving days after floods killed and displaced people in the capital, Accra.

The gathering blended grief with faith as a shaken country tried to find its footing again.

Economic worries linger

Mahama admitted that many young people remain jobless and that businesses struggle to borrow money affordably.

Prices rose to 5.3 percent in June, and the tax filing deadline was pushed back to July 6 after the floods.

Senegal – Heartbreak at the World Cup

A lead thrown away

Senegal led Belgium 2-0 until the 85th minute before losing 3-2 in extra time on a disputed penalty by Youri Tielemans.

The collapse left fans and players heartbroken and furious in equal measure.

Anger boils over

Midfielder Pape Gueye announced he is stepping away from the national team over the coaching staff.

Supporters slammed coach Pape Thiaw’s substitutions, and three pitch invaders briefly halted play.

Morocco – The Atlas Lions Roar On

Nerves of steel

Morocco beat the Netherlands 3-2 on penalties after Issa Diop scored a dramatic equaliser deep into stoppage time.

Goalkeeper Yassine Bounou made the crucial save that set up Ismael Saibari’s winning spot-kick.

Africa’s flagbearer

The team, known as the Atlas Lions, now carries much of the continent’s hope into the last 16.

They face Canada in Houston on Saturday, with a whole nation cheering behind them.

Sudan – Battlefield Shifts Amid War

Ground gained

Army-aligned Joint Forces captured the town of Kulbus in West Darfur, close to the border with Chad.

Air defences also shot down a drone over Tendelti in White Nile State, small signs of momentum.

Grave warnings

Amnesty International accused the Rapid Support Forces of crimes against humanity and possible genocide in North Darfur.

Yet there was a flicker of normal life as Qatar Airways launched its first flight to Port Sudan.

The Bigger Picture The overriding feeling across Africa today is emotional whiplash. Morocco’s shootout triumph and the memory of earlier football joy sit uneasily beside Senegal’s collapse, Ghana’s floods and the rising Ebola dead in DR Congo. Politics is where the anger burns brightest. South Africans are livid over a disgraced minister’s return, migrants are fleeing unrest that now strains ties with Nigeria and Mozambique, and Angola’s ruling party faces its most turbulent year in memory. Beneath it all runs a quieter, weary resilience. From Ghana’s prayer day to Kenya’s cheer over county funds and Egypt’s small relief on prices, people are leaning on faith, family and football to keep going.

What We Are Watching

Today – WHO and DR Congo publish their weekly Ebola report, showing whether the outbreak is being contained.

This week – Morocco face Canada in Houston on Saturday as Africa’s last strong World Cup hope.

This week – Ghana’s extended tax filing deadline arrives on July 6 after the Accra floods.

This week – US independence references ripple across the Sahel as those states reaffirm shifting Western ties.

This week – Nigeria and South Africa open compensation talks over the migrant crisis fallout.

Later this month – Angola’s interior ministry opens online recruitment on July 16 amid jobs pressure.

Later this month – An Angolan influencer’s retrial on July 17 tests civic space and press freedom.

Ahead – South Sudan’s December election looms as Kenya’s Ruto urges inclusive dialogue.

Frequently Asked Questions

How bad is the Ebola outbreak in DR Congo right now?

Over 400 people have died and there are 1,406 confirmed cases of the Bundibugyo strain, with nearly a third of those infected dying. President Tshisekedi has announced a 319 million dollar response plan, backed by 910 million dollars in donor pledges.

What happened during South Africa's anti-migrant protests?

More than 900 people were arrested during Tuesday's nationwide protests, which included looting at some of the 120 marches held. The unrest caused thousands of migrants to flee, with over 7,000 undocumented Malawians sent home after a shelter in Pietermaritzburg closed.

How far has Morocco gone in the tournament and who do they play next?

Morocco beat the Netherlands 3-2 on penalties to reach the last 16, with goalkeeper Yassine Bounou making the crucial save that led to the winning spot-kick. They face Canada in Houston on Saturday.

North America feels split down the middle, with American birthday pride bumping against jittery markets and an immigration fight in the courts. Canada answers with a defiant, worried patriotism as storms and a trade snub test its calm.

(Photo internet reproduction)

USA/Canada – Trade Pact Snub

No renewal

US Trade Representative Jamieson Greer said Washington will not renew the North American trade pact, known as USMCA in the US and CUSMA in Canada, in its current form.

The deal stays in force until 2036, but it now faces yearly reviews that could reopen its biggest terms at any point.

What is at stake

The pact covers roughly 1.3 trillion dollars in trade between the three countries, and it shields about 90 percent of Canadian exports.

The US ran a goods deficit with Canada of 46 billion dollars last year, and the two neighbours have not yet begun their own direct talks.

Canada – A Rained-Out Canada Day

Unity message

Prime Minister Mark Carney urged Canadians to stay united as the country marked 159 years since Confederation, its founding as a nation.

Speaking in French, he offered a line meant to reassure a divided country: unity does not require uniformity.

Storms take over

A severe thunderstorm forced Ottawa to cancel its evening celebration and fireworks, and it also scrapped Carney’s planned speech in Edmonton.

The capital sat under both a thunderstorm watch and a heat alert, a fitting image for a nation feeling both proud and strained.

“Unity does not require uniformity,” Prime Minister Mark Carney told a rained-out nation on Canada Day.

Canada – Alberta’s Pipeline Gamble

A big plan

Alberta Premier Danielle Smith is set to detail a pipeline that could carry up to one million barrels of oil a day to the West Coast.

The proposal is being floated without a private company behind it, according to reporting by the Globe and Mail.

Timing and tension

The plan is tied to the Pathways project, which aims to capture and store carbon, and the earliest digging would begin on September 1, 2027.

It arrives just before Alberta’s referendum on October 19, which includes a question on leaving Canada, raising the stakes for national unity.

USA – Stocks Rise as Hiring Cools

A softer jobs report

US employers added only 57,000 jobs in June, far short of the 113,000 forecast, ending a three-month run of strong hiring.

The unemployment rate stood at 4.2 percent, a cooler reading that many welcomed.

Why markets liked it

The gentler numbers support the Federal Reserve, the US central bank, holding interest rates steady while leaving a later increase possible, and the Dow rose about half a percent.

Markets closed early on Thursday and stay shut on Friday for the July 4 holiday.

USA – World Cup Breakthrough

A gritty win

The US men’s football team beat Bosnia 2-0 in Santa Clara to reach the last 16 of the World Cup.

Folarin Balogun scored his third goal of the tournament, then was controversially sent off, leaving his side to finish with ten players.

What comes next

Malik Tillman sealed the win with a free kick, giving the US its first World Cup knockout victory since 2002.

The team now faces Belgium on July 6 in Seattle, though Balogun’s red card rules him out of that match.

USA – Birthright Fight Widens

Court ruling

The Supreme Court upheld birthright citizenship, the rule that grants citizenship to nearly everyone born on US soil, handing the Trump administration its third recent loss.

The 6-3 conservative court, which includes three Trump-appointed justices, sided against the White House.

New crackdown

Officials say they will now deny visas to pregnant travellers and prosecute operators of so-called birth tourism, where people travel to give birth in the US.

Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin described the practice as a national security risk.

USA – A 250th Birthday Nears

Semiquincentennial

The United States celebrates 250 years of independence on July 4, a milestone known as the semiquincentennial.

New York will host Sail250, a gathering of about 60 ships from 30 countries billed as the largest US maritime event.

Mood and critics

The original Declaration of Independence, penned by Thomas Jefferson, goes on view at the New York Public Library from July 1 to 3.

Some official events have drawn criticism for feeling political and for a lack of clarity about how they are funded.

Canada – Quebec Election on the Horizon

A vote looms

Quebec heads to a general election on October 5, with the pro-independence Parti Québécois currently leading in the polls at about 31 percent.

Premier Christine Fréchette’s governing party has recovered some support since she took over.

The sovereignty question

The election revives the long-running debate over whether Quebec should become its own country, championed by PQ leader Paul St-Pierre Plamondon.

Yet polls suggest most Quebecers still oppose the idea, with about 63 percent against sovereignty.

The Bigger Picture North America is living a split-screen moment: the United States swings between birthday pride and unease over softer jobs, a shaky market open and a courtroom fight over who counts as a citizen. Canada answers with a defiant patriotism that storms literally shut down on Canada Day. The thread tying it all together is the relationship between the two neighbours. Trump’s refusal to renew the shared trade pact lands as Alberta and Quebec each edge toward votes that question their place in Canada, sharpening a national-unity worry that had been simmering for months. Amid the tension, sport offered a rare shared jolt of joy, as the US men’s football team ground out a knockout win. It is a reminder that even a jittery region still finds moments to cheer together.

What We Are Watching

Today – Alberta Premier Smith details her West Coast pipeline plan.

Today – Quebec Premier Fréchette makes a home-ownership announcement as housing dominates the campaign.

Today – The US bond market closes early ahead of the holiday.

July 3 – US markets shut for the Independence Day holiday.

July 4 – The US marks its 250th birthday with Sail250 in New York.

July 6 – The US men face Belgium in the World Cup last 16 in Seattle, without the suspended Balogun.

July 10 – Statistics Canada releases its June jobs figures before the next rate decision.

October – Quebec votes on October 5 and Alberta holds its referendum on October 19.

Europe is torn between pride and dread today, cheering an Italian tech triumph while bracing for another punishing heat spell in the south. Governments in Berlin and Madrid try to project control, but weary and sceptical publics are not easily won over.

Football deepens the mood, with Dutch heartbreak and German embarrassment set against celebration elsewhere. Behind the headlines runs a quiet worry that record heat is becoming the new normal.

Germany – A Reform Leap Forward

An overnight deal

Germany’s governing coalition, led by Chancellor Friedrich Merz, agreed overnight on a sweeping package covering income taxes, pensions and cuts to red tape. The details were unveiled at a 9 am press conference and hailed as a big leap forward.

At the heart sits ten billion euros in income-tax relief starting on 1 January 2027, easing the load for low and middle earners. A typical family could keep up to 600 euros more each year.

The catch that stings

Not everyone is cheering, as telephone sick-notes will be scrapped and a doctor’s certificate required from the very first day of illness. Family doctors called that change catastrophic.

The small-job flat tax will rise from two to five percent, and a planned savings-based pension could lift contributions by up to two percentage points. Unions attacked wider use of short-term work contracts as an unnecessary cut.

Italy – A Global Tech Champion

A blockbuster debut

Milan-based software firm Bending Spoons made a dazzling entrance on the Nasdaq, the American technology stock market. It priced its shares at 29 dollars each, above the expected range, and raised about 1.68 billion dollars.

The shares then jumped, closing the first day up nearly 40 percent at 40.50 dollars. That pushed the company’s value past 24 billion dollars.

Why it matters

It is billed as the first fully digital Italian software firm to list on the Nasdaq, and many see it as proof that Italy can build a global technology champion. National pride is running high.

The four founders keep about 48 percent of the company and 82 percent of the voting power through special shares. Chief executive Luca Ferrari led the effort.

A right-wing head of state is ‘no longer a taboo’ — Giorgia Meloni.

France – Bracing For More Heat

A record spell ends

France is finally leaving behind a brutal heat spell that ran from 17 June to 2 July. The 24th and 25th of June were the hottest days ever recorded there, with the daily average first reaching 30 degrees.

Saintes hit a peak of 43.8 degrees, and the strain on health has been severe. Heat claimed 5,722 lives in France in 2025.

No respite in sight

The national weather service warns temperatures will climb again from Thursday in the south, spreading nationwide by the weekend. At some supermarkets, shoppers rushed in near-chaotic scenes to buy air conditioners before the next hot stretch.

Fires have flared, with a blaze in the Minervois area spreading to nearly 950 hectares. Exhaustion and anxiety are settling in as this feels like the new normal.

Netherlands – Penalty Heartbreak Returns

Out on spot-kicks

The Dutch national team crashed out of the World Cup, losing a penalty shootout to Morocco after a 1-1 draw. Kluivert, Timber and Summerville all missed from the spot.

It is the seventh time the team has been knocked out of a major tournament on penalties. The pain of an old wound has reopened.

A coach in doubt

Afterwards, coach Ronald Koeman openly questioned his own future. The mood in the football world turned to self-criticism and gloom.

Fans in Amsterdam drifted home disillusioned, while Moroccan supporters celebrated in a lively district of The Hague. The country is half-mourning a golden generation.

Spain – Party Locked Down

Snap internal votes

Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez’s party has called quick internal elections in five regional branches plus Madrid, to be held in July. The aim is to shield candidates loyal to the leadership before the 2027 vote.

The move followed a surprise Madrid bid by Enma Lopez, which led to her forced departure from the party’s national executive. A first round is set for 19 July, with a possible run-off on 26 July.

Courts circle the family

Meanwhile, prosecutors opposed a request by the prime minister’s wife, Begona Gomez, to travel abroad from 7 to 10 July, citing a risk she might flee justice. She wants to join him at a summit in Ankara and attend her daughter’s graduation in London.

A judge had earlier taken her passport and barred her from leaving Spain ahead of a jury trial on four alleged offences. Separately, police searched a provincial-council building in Cadiz over secret contracts.

Germany – Doctors And Unions Push Back

A revolt over sick-notes

Family doctors branded the plan to require a certificate from the first day of illness absolutely catastrophic. The change is the most contested part of the new package.

The country’s main union group attacked the widened use of short-term job contracts as an unnecessary cut. Such contracts could be extended up to six times and last up to 48 months until the end of 2030.

Football under a cloud

Separately, prosecutors launched nationwide raids over suspected corruption tied to discounted football tickets. The inquiry centres on tickets allegedly sold at preferential prices.

It lands amid heavy coverage of Germany’s own World Cup exit to Paraguay. The timing has deepened a sense of embarrassment around the game.

Portugal – On Edge Under Red Alerts

Fire fears mount

Twelve districts have been placed on red heat warnings from Thursday to Saturday as temperatures climb. Authorities warned the conditions for severe fires are enormous.

Air-force planes have been sent to help stand ready. The public is wary and on edge.

A sour note in sport

A refereeing scandal has shaken Portuguese football, with the resignation of official Duarte Gomes and the opening of an inquiry. It has soured an already tense mood.

The combination of heat fear and sporting controversy leaves the country uneasy. Summer here feels heavy this year.

Italy – The Presidency Becomes A Battle

A taboo lifted

Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni argued on television that a right-wing head of state is no longer a taboo if her side wins again. She framed the 2029 presidential vote as a live campaign fight.

Names such as Mantovano and Crosetto are already circulating as possible centre-right contenders. Her trust rating stands at 42 percent, with 61 percent approving her foreign policy.

The opposition fires back

Opposition figures accused her of unmasking a real aim to seize the presidency. Former prime minister Matteo Renzi vowed to stop her run, calling her ministers unfit and pledging to send her home.

The exchange has turned bitter and personal. Italy’s politics now feel like a permanent campaign.

The Bigger Picture Europe today is a study in contrasts, with Italy basking in the glow of a global tech success while much of the south braces for yet another spell of extreme heat. That heat, following the most intense western European heatwave on record, is feeding a deeper anxiety that such summers are here to stay. Governments are trying to look steady. Berlin promotes a bold reform as a leap forward even as doctors and unions object, while Madrid rallies its party as courts investigate the prime minister’s family. In both cases, the public feels weary and doubtful rather than reassured. Football, as so often, mirrors the emotional swing of the continent. Dutch heartbreak and lingering German embarrassment sit alongside pride and celebration elsewhere, a reminder of how closely the game is woven into national feeling.

What We Are Watching

Today – Germany’s coalition presents the full reform detail, reshaping household finances from 2027.

Today – Bending Spoons trading continues on the Nasdaq after its near-40 percent first-day jump.

Today – Spain and France play World Cup knockout matches that will swing national moods.

This week – A new heat spell builds over France, Spain and Portugal, with red alerts spreading.

This week – The contested travel window for Begona Gomez around 7 to 10 July tests a judge’s limits.

This week – The Spanish party’s signature-collection window for its snap votes opens from 4 July.

19 July – First round of the Spanish party’s snap internal elections, notably in Madrid.

End of 2026 – Germany aims to pass pension recommendations, including a savings-based pension, into law.

How much money will German workers actually save under the new tax deal?

Low and middle earners will get ten billion euros in income-tax relief starting 1 January 2027, and a typical family could keep up to 600 euros more each year.

How did Bending Spoons' stock market debut go?

The Milan-based software firm priced its shares at 29 dollars each, then closed its first day on the Nasdaq up nearly 40 percent at 40.50 dollars, pushing its total value past 24 billion dollars.

How bad has the heat been in France this summer?

The 24th and 25th of June were the hottest days ever recorded in France, with Saintes hitting a peak of 43.8 degrees, and heat claimed 5,722 lives there in 2025.

Beneath the sport, India’s market climbed and China’s plants got busier again. Yet bombings in southern Thailand and abuse scandals in Indonesia kept an anxious undertow running through the day.

Japan – A Grateful Homecoming

Fans line the airport

Japan’s players flew home on July 2 after losing 1-2 to Brazil in the last 32 of the World Cup, arriving on three separate flights into Tokyo’s two main airports.

Around 500 supporters and 100 reporters met the first arrivals at Narita, chanting and calling out ‘Japan, thank you’ as the squad walked through.

A coach in limbo

At an evening press conference in Tokyo, coach Hajime Moriyasu said the team’s ‘phase in the world has changed’ and vowed ‘the future is definitely world number one’.

The football association is expected to make an unusual one-year contract offer ahead of the Asian Cup in Saudi Arabia in January, leaving his future briefly uncertain.

South Korea – Anger and Shame

A historic collapse

South Korea crashed out at the group stage after losing to Mexico and South Africa, sliding to 32nd in the world ranking, its lowest in four and a half years.

Commentators called the defeat to South Africa the worst national-team game of the century, and the squad’s planned homecoming event was cancelled.

The coach walks away

Coach Hong Myung-bo announced his resignation at a press conference in Mexico, closing a painful chapter for the team.

The 26-player squad still receives bonuses totalling about 2.08 billion won, a sum that has drawn fresh irritation from disappointed fans.

“The future is definitely world number one,” Japan’s coach vowed, even in the sting of defeat.

India – Markets Ride the Optimism

A confident day of trading

The Sensex index of leading shares jumped 579 points to 77,502 on July 2, while the technology sector had its best day in about 14 months.

Gains came as oil prices eased on hopeful signs from United States-Iran talks and gentler comments from the American central bank.

Eyes on Japan ties

Investors pointed to hopes around the India-Japan summit, watching for deals on trade, defence, computer chips and artificial intelligence.

The rupee, India’s currency, softened a little to around 95.36 to the United States dollar, but that did not dent the day’s cheer.

Vietnam – A Half-Century Milestone

Fifty years of a name

Leader To Lam spoke on July 2 at the Reunification Hall marking 50 years since Saigon was renamed Ho Chi Minh City in 1976.

He urged planners to keep a ‘hundred-year, far-sighted vision’ so that today’s choices do not block tomorrow’s growth.

New laws touch daily life

From July 1, about 3.5 million pensioners saw their payments rise by 8 percent, with extra help for the lowest earners.

A special tax on petrol returned the same day, while a broader fuel-tax cut stays in place until the end of September.

China – Factories Find Their Feet

Back in growth

China’s official factory gauge rose to 50.3 in June, staying above the line that separates growth from decline for a fourth month in a row.

New orders climbed and export orders returned to growth, easing some of the anxiety around the wider economy.

Uneven strength

High-technology manufacturing was especially strong, with analysts crediting industries tied to artificial intelligence.

Yet small firms remained weak, and analysts warned of downward pressure in the second half of the year.

Indonesia – Relief and Outrage

Cheaper fuel at the pump

State firm Pertamina cut prices for several non-subsidised fuels from early July, easing pressure on drivers’ wallets.

The cheaper prices for subsidised fuels used by most households were left unchanged, and the company linked the move to world oil prices and public spending power.

Scandals stir anger

Police in Depok named a father and son as suspects in the sexual abuse of students at a religious boarding school in Bogor.

Separately, anti-graft officers detained the second wife of a regent tied to a bribery case, keeping public anger simmering.

Thailand – Unease in the South

Bombings return

The government is stepping up its response after a series of bomb attacks reignited violence in Thailand’s southernmost provinces.

Prime Minister Anutin Charnvirakul is set to meet Malaysian leaders on July 9-10 to seek solutions to the long-running unrest.

A hand to migrants

The cabinet approved a one-year extension of a scheme covering the legal status of long-term migrants, now running to June 30, 2027.

The move offers some steadiness at a moment when the mood in the deep south feels tense and unsettled.

Philippines – Tense Civic Energy

A permit pulled

Quezon City revoked the rally permit granted to the religious group Iglesia ni Cristo for Thursday, July 2.

Police urged protesters to comply with the conditions of any permit, sharpening the political atmosphere in the city.

A regional role

The Philippines continues as this year’s chair of the Southeast Asian bloc, coordinating the observer team on the Thailand-Cambodia border.

That mandate runs to July 2026, keeping Manila busy managing tensions well beyond its own streets.

The Bigger Picture Asia woke on July 2 split between the pitch and the wallet. The World Cup dominated hearts, with Japan returning home to grateful cheers and South Korea to angry silence after a historic collapse. Away from the football, there was quiet relief. India’s market climbed on falling oil, China’s factories grew for a fourth straight month, and cheaper fuel in Indonesia and Vietnam gently eased the cost of daily life. Yet the calm was not complete. Bombings in southern Thailand, abuse scandals in Indonesia, protest tension in the Philippines and an approaching storm over northern Vietnam all kept a thread of worry running beneath the day.

What We Are Watching

Today – Moriyasu’s press conference signals whether he stays on for January’s Asian Cup.

Today – Quezon City protest tensions after the revoked rally permit.

This week – Australia meets Egypt on July 3, the last Asian side left in the knockout rounds.

This week – A tropical depression may become the season’s first storm, threatening heavy rain in northern Vietnam.

This week – Anutin’s July 9-10 talks with Malaysian leaders over southern-Thailand violence.

This week – Vietnam’s petrol tax changes take hold, affecting household and business costs.

Ahead – India’s university admission registration opens for millions of students.

Ahead – The World Cup final on July 19 at MetLife Stadium in New Jersey.

World.title: São Paulo Nightlife Tonight — July 2, 2026
World.content:

São Paulo · Nightlife

If You Only Go to One Place Ó do Borogodó If you do one thing tonight, squeeze into this tiny Pinheiros samba house. Since 2001 it has hosted the most important names in samba, choro and Brazilian rhythms — a simple house with the best music in the city, and it is a Thursday-perfect night: locals dancing centimetres from the band, cold beer, zero tourist gloss. Concerts start around midnight and Thursdays are among the best nights — arrive by 10.30 pm for a table and let São Paulo happen to you.

Tonight at a Glance —Ó do Borogodó The real samba roda, all ages of paulistanos dancing tight; every night, but Thursday is a sweet spot — arrive 10.30 pm, music peaks after midnight —D-Edge World-ranked electronic club in Barra Funda; serious dancers and international heads — its weekly party Moving runs every Thursday, so tonight is its night —Bar Brahma Live samba and MPB on the most famous corner in São Paulo; mixed locals, visitors, old bohemians — open Thursday till 2 am, go for the 8-9 pm show slot —Villa Country Brazil’s most famous sertanejo palace, boots and all; young, flirty, very Brazilian crowd — Thursdays from 8 pm, and tonight it also hosts the Anime Friends Hotzone party —Tokyo 東京 Nine floors of karaoke, DJs and a neon rooftop facing the Copan; young, queer-friendly, alternative — Thursdays 5 pm to 5 am, ideal after everything else shuts

It’s Thursday 2 July 2026 and São Paulo is mid-World-Cup-winter and fully awake: Moving takes over D-Edge as it does every Thursday, Anime Friends’ opening-day Hotzone party lands at Villa Country at 8 pm, and the Arena Brasileira festival is still running in Ibirapuera with Cup screenings and big-name shows through 19 July. The classic circuit: boteco beers at 8 pm, live music around 10, samba at Ó do Borogodó near midnight, then Barra Funda’s dancefloors until the birds sing.

Tonight across Sao Paulo. (Photo internet reproduction)

What’s On Tonight

Moving — D-Edge’s resident Thursday club night (house/techno) — at D-Edge, Barra Funda, From around 11 pm. Moving happens every Thursday at D-EDGE, one of São Paulo’s most renowned electronic clubs, which hosts big names from the scene weekly — tonight is the proper club night of the week

Anime Friends Hotzone — official party of Latin America’s biggest pop-Asian festival — at Villa Country, Água Branca, Doors 8 pm. The Anime Friends Hotzone runs tonight, Thursday 2 July, with doors at 8 pm at Villa Country, as Anime Friends itself runs 2–5 July — a gloriously odd one-off in the sertanejo temple

Arena Brasileira — World Cup fan festival with match screens and Brazilian headliners — at Parque Ibirapuera (Portão 10), Evening; hours track the football. Running until 19 July in Ibirapuera, it mixes live Cup screenings with shows from a line-up including Ivete Sangalo, Anitta, Marisa Monte, Caetano Veloso, Thiaguinho and Péricles across the period — check tonight’s bill on ingresse.com/arenabrasileira

Samba and choro roda — the nightly house band and guests — at Ó do Borogodó, Pinheiros, Doors ~9 pm; music builds to midnight. Live music daily — samba raiz, choro and batuque; the weekday roda is where you actually dance with locals

Live samba/MPB on the Ipiranga × São João corner — at Bar Brahma, Centro, Shows through the evening; open till 2 am. July’s programme at Bar Brahma Centro is packed with established shows, tributes and samba on São Paulo’s most famous corner — the easiest first-night wow in the city

Zizi Possi residency (voice and piano) — or tonight’s headline set — at Blue Note São Paulo, Av. Paulista, Evening sets; arrive at doors for a good table. Zizi Possi returns to the Blue Note São Paulo stage in June and July 2026 for exclusive voice-and-piano shows; check @bluenotesp for tonight’s exact bill — tables are first-come, so the earlier you arrive the better the view

Thursday karaoke at the fervo’s favourite pop club — at Bofetada Club, Jardim Paulista/Frei Caneca, Late evening. Open-bar entry nights and karaoke that usually lands on Thursdays — the friendliest low-stakes LGBTQ+ start to the night

Rooftop DJs and all-floors karaoke — at Tokyo 東京, Vila Buarque, 5 pm–5 am. Its programme is versatile and progressive, with celebrated São Paulo DJs and parties and Thursday hours run 5 pm to 5 am — the reliable late-late landing spot tonight

The Circuit: When to Go Where

Warm up 8 pm — boteco beers and petiscos in Pinheiros/Vila Madalena, or a chopp at Bar Brahma’s corner in Centro; Brazilians eat and drink first, dance later

10 pm — a proper show: Blue Note on Paulista for jazz/MPB elegance, or Bar Brahma’s salon for old-school samba; both are calm, safe, solo-friendly

11.30 pm — cross to Ó do Borogodó in Pinheiros: the concerts start around midnight, which is exactly when São Paulo wakes up

After midnight — Moving at D-Edge, tonight’s Thursday club institution in Barra Funda; take a 99/Uber, it’s not a walking area

Still going at 3 am — Tokyo’s rooftop in Vila Buarque pours until 5 am on Thursdays; karaoke shame is optional

LGBTQ+ branch line — start on Rua Frei Caneca, the core gay district with bars, clubs and street life clustered together, with Bofetada’s Thursday karaoke as tonight’s anchor

Scenes & Sounds

Samba — Acoustic rodas where the crowd sings every word; sweaty, joyful, physical Where: Ó do Borogodó in Pinheiros, Bar Brahma in Centro, plus Boteco da Dona Tati in Barra Funda, which honours the old guards and historic composers

MPB — Seated, candle-lit, listening-room Brazil — goosebump territory Where: Casa de Francisca in the old centre and Blue Note São Paulo on Paulista

Electronic — São Paulo is one of the world’s most relevant electronic cities, with demanding crowds and serious sound investment Where: D-Edge in Barra Funda, once voted among the best clubs in the world, and the smaller, more intimate Clash Club for techno and house

Sertanejo — Brazilian country-pop, danced in pairs, boots and big choruses; it lotta (it packs out) Where: Villa Country, arguably the most famous sertanejo club in Brazil, Água Branca

Funk — Baile funk starts later and runs till morning — bass-heavy, euphoric, very carioca-meets-paulista Where: Audio Club’s programme often includes funk and pagode-funk nights with big structure and a central location, plus roving centre parties (find them on Instagram)

Forró — Accordion-led partner dancing from the northeast; strangers will teach you the steps Where: Templo – Bar de Fé, where forró takes over the house on Fridays — bookmark it for tomorrow

Pick Your Night

Date night: Casa de Francisca — a gilded music salon in the historic Palacete Teresa in the centre; book dinner-and-show seats on its site and arrive when the room opens

Solo and safe: Blue Note São Paulo — inside the Conjunto Nacional on Av. Paulista, 200 m from Consolação metro; table service, no awkwardness, world-class stage

Dance till sunrise: D-Edge for Moving, then Tokyo’s rooftop — open till 5 am on Thursdays

Meet locals: Ó do Borogodó — tables are shared, the dancefloor is a handkerchief, and you should arrive early because tables are hotly disputed

Meet other expats: Vila Madalena’s bar corners (Aspicuelta × Mourato Coelho) for the warm-up, then Tokyo — both are English-friendly and easy to strike up conversation

Where to Go

Ó do Borogodó — Pinheiros (Vila Madalena edge) Since 2001 the home of samba, choro and Brazilian rhythms, old and new generations, in a simple house with the best music in the city; crowd is all-ages paulistano with a sprinkling of in-the-know foreigners Tonight: Reliable nightly roda — Thursday is one of the classic nights; music builds towards midnight Best time: Wednesdays, Thursdays and weekends have the best atmosphere; weekdays are better for dancing freely. Doors ~9 pm; arrive by 10.30 pm for a table, expect to leave at 2–3 am Cost: Modest door cover (historically in the R$20–40 range) plus cheap bottled beer; bring some cash as backup Address: Rua Horácio Lane, 21, Pinheiros Website: odoborogododotbar.wordpress.com Getting there: Short 99/Uber from anywhere in Pinheiros/Vila Madalena; Fradique Coutinho metro then 10-min walk Good to know: No bookings — queue and squeeze in; dress casual, dancing shoes

D-Edge — Barra Funda A world reference in electronic music — high-definition sound, impeccable curation and Muti Randolph’s futurist light-grid design; serious clubbers, DJs, art kids, international visitors Tonight: Moving, the house Thursday party — from ~11 pm till very late Best time: Runs Thursday to Saturday with big national and international names weekly; go after midnight, peak 2–4 am. Two dancefloors, a lounge and a terrace with a city view Cost: Ticketed entry (buy online in advance; prices vary by line-up); drinks on a card comanda; cards accepted Address: Av. Mário de Andrade, 141, Barra Funda Website: www.d-edge.com.br Getting there: 99/Uber recommended; near Palmeiras-Barra Funda station for the way in Good to know: Buy tickets ahead on the club’s channels; dress dark and comfortable, no beachwear

Bar Brahma — Centro (República) An icon of paulistano bohemia since 1948, on the famous Ipiranga × São João corner immortalised in the song ‘Sampa’; it stages old-guard samba and MPB in its main salon — around 1,500 performances a year. Crowd: everyone from grandads to first dates Tonight: Live music standby every night in July — the month’s programme mixes established shows, original projects, tributes and samba Best time: Thursday to Saturday 11 am–2 am; arrive 8–9 pm for dinner and the first set Cost: Couvert artístico added on show nights plus your food/drink tab; cards and Pix accepted; chopp is the classic order Address: Av. São João, 677 (corner of Av. Ipiranga), Centro Instagram: @barbrahma Website: www.barbrahmasp.com Getting there: República metro (Linha 3-Vermelha/4-Amarela), 3-min walk; 99/Uber to the door late at night Good to know: Book a table online for headline shows; smart-casual, easygoing door

Blue Note São Paulo — Av. Paulista / Consolação The New York club’s São Paulo outpost, inside the Conjunto Nacional with a view over Avenida Paulista — jazz, MPB and samba royalty in supper-club comfort; grown-up, polished crowd, very solo-friendly Tonight: Zizi Possi’s voice-and-piano residency runs June–July 2026; confirm tonight’s bill on @bluenotesp before you go Best time: Any night there’s a show you like; doors before the set — seating is first-come, and the earlier you arrive the better the stage view Cost: Ticketed per show (sold via Eventim/site), plus food and drinks; cards accepted Address: Av. Paulista, 2073, 2º andar (Conjunto Nacional), Consolação Instagram: @bluenotesp Website: bluenotesp.com Getting there: 200 m from Consolação metro (green line) Good to know: Yes — buy show tickets ahead; smart casual

Tokyo 東京 — Vila Buarque / Centro Bars, karaoke, music and a restaurant stacked in a nine-floor building with a rooftop dancefloor and terrace looking onto the Edifício Itália and Copan; young, alternative, strongly LGBTQIA+-friendly with an inclusive programme and crowd Tonight: Reliable Thursday standby: DJs upstairs, collective karaoke below, kitchen late Best time: Tue–Thu 5 pm–5 am, Fri till 6 am; go 10 pm for dinner-karaoke or 2 am to keep the night alive Cost: Door entry usually ~R$25–40 depending on the night; private karaoke rooms from R$100/hour; cards accepted Address: R. Major Sertório, 110, Vila Buarque Phone: +55 11 3159-0190 Instagram: @tokyo.sp Website: tokyo011.com.br Getting there: República metro, 5-min walk; 99/Uber late Good to know: No table reservations — first come, first served; 18+ only and original photo ID (passport fine) is mandatory

Villa Country — Água Branca / Barra Funda The most famous sertanejo club in Brazil, decked out Wild-West style across 12,000 m² of showroom, restaurant, dancefloor, billiards, seven bars and more; crowd is flirty, dressed-up, 20s–40s, genuinely Brazilian Tonight: Anime Friends Hotzone tonight, Thursday 2 July, doors 8 pm — layered onto its regular Thursday-night opening Best time: Thu, Fri, Sat and Sun from 8 pm; arrive 9–10 pm, dance classes and warm-up before headliners Cost: Ticketed entry via Ticket360 (varies by night/artist); drinks on comanda; cards fine Address: Av. Francisco Matarazzo, 774, Água Branca Instagram: @villacountry Website: villacountry.com.br Getting there: Palmeiras-Barra Funda metro/CPTM then short walk or 99/Uber Good to know: Buy tickets ahead for show nights; jeans-and-boots dress code is optional but fun; 18+

Casa de Francisca — Sé / Centro Histórico Installed since 2017 in the Palacete Teresa, one of the most emblematic addresses in paulistano cultural history and considered one of the most significant music spaces in São Paulo; a candle-lit listening room for MPB, samba and new Brazilian music — date-night gold Tonight: Check the site’s July agenda for tonight’s porão or salão show; a typical night runs doors 7.30 pm, show 9.30–11 pm, close at 1 am Best time: Weeknights are magical and easier to book; arrive at doors to settle in with dinner Cost: Ticketed per show via the official site (some nights have free early allocations); dinner and drinks on your tab; cards accepted Address: Rua Quintino Bocaiúva, 22, Sé Website: casadefrancisca.art.br Getting there: Sé or São Bento metro then short walk; take a 99/Uber to the door at night Good to know: Yes — reserve ahead online, shows sell out; smart casual

Bofetada Club — Jardim Paulista / Frei Caneca corridor A popular disco-club with DJs, a lively dancefloor and a festive vibe at the heart of the LGBTQ+ strip; young, mixed, zero-attitude crowd Tonight: Entry usually comes with open bar, and Thursdays generally mean karaoke Best time: Thu for karaoke; Fri–Sat for the full party; things ignite after 11 pm Cost: Entry with open bar on many nights; drinks and vodka/whisky-energy combos otherwise; cards accepted Address: Rua Peixoto Gomide, 131, Jardim Paulista Phone: +55 11 93932-6218 Instagram: @bofetadaclub Getting there: Between Paulista and Baixo Augusta; Consolação metro then walk, or 99/Uber Good to know: No booking needed; free-spirited dress, 18+ with ID

Blue Space — Barra Funda One of Brazil’s most iconic gay clubs — the drag shows alone are worth the trip, massive productions with lights and choreography; the biggest and most famous, with Broadway-level productions Tonight: Weekend-focused — treat it as your Saturday plan; tonight stick to Frei Caneca and come back for the drag spectacular Best time: Saturday nights, arriving after midnight for the main show Cost: Ticketed entry varying by night; drinks on comanda; cards accepted Address: Rua Brigadeiro Galvão, 723, Barra Funda Instagram: @bluespacesp Getting there: 99/Uber door-to-door recommended in Barra Funda at night Good to know: Tickets ahead for big drag nights; dress to be seen; 18+

Neighbourhoods at a Glance

Vila Madalena / Pinheiros: Bar-crawl central — corner botecos, samba dens and craft beer; the easiest place to start talking to strangers, locals and expats alike

Baixo Augusta / Consolação (incl. Rua Frei Caneca): The city’s anything-goes strip — indie clubs, drag, rock dives; the Frei Caneca region is a central axis of the LGBTQ+ scene with wildly different nights side by side

Centro: República / Vila Buarque / Sé: Old São Paulo glamour reborn — historic bars, listening rooms and rooftops; electric but keep your phone pocketed on the walk

Barra Funda: Warehouse-land of the mega-nights — D-Edge, Villa Country and Blue Space all cluster here; arrive and leave by app car

Itaim Bibi / Vila Olímpia: Suits-off finance crowd, cocktail bars and glossy clubs — pricier drinks, easier English, dressier doors

LGBTQ+ Tonight

Bofetada Club — DJs, a packed dancefloor and a festive, welcoming crowd on the Frei Caneca strip — and tonight is its usual Thursday karaoke

Blue Space — The biggest and most famous LGBTQ+ club, with Broadway-level drag productions in Barra Funda — best on weekends after midnight

Casa Fluida — A much-praised, inclusive bar known for its vibrant, welcoming atmosphere with live drag shows and art exhibitions on Rua Bela Cintra — perfect early-evening tonight

Money & How Paying Works The comanda: at most bars and clubs you’re handed a card or paper slip at the door; every drink goes on it and you pay everything at a caixa (till) on the way out. Guard it with your life — losing it usually means paying a hefty flat fine, often R$100–300. Couvert artístico: live-music venues add a per-person music cover (typically R$15–50) to your bill — it’s the band’s fee, not a scam. Ticketed clubs charge entry (entrada) instead, cheaper if bought online or via a lista (guest list on Instagram/WhatsApp). Cards and Pix are accepted almost everywhere — Brazil is very tap-to-pay — but carry R$50–100 in cash for small samba houses, cloakrooms and street snacks. Tipping: 10% (the serviço) is usually already on the bill; just check the receipt. No extra tip expected, though rounding up for good service is warm-hearted.

Getting Home Safe

The metro runs from about 4.40 am until midnight — fine for getting TO the party, useless for getting home after it. A 24-hour Saturday pilot on lines 1, 2, 3 and 15 ran into 2026, but tonight is Thursday: plan on an app car.

Use 99 or Uber, never a street-hailed taxi at 3 am. Ask the door staff where the safe pickup point is (big clubs like D-Edge and Villa Country have marked zones), wait inside or with the bouncer, and check the plate before getting in.

Surge is real at closing time — either leave 20 minutes before the lights come on, or have one last água com gás and let prices settle. Split fares with new friends heading the same way.

São Paulo at night is mostly about phone-sense, not fear: keep it in a front pocket, don’t walk and text, and don’t wander empty centre blocks alone after midnight — take the R$15 ride instead. Inside venues you’re very well looked after.

Pace the caipirinhas, keep an eye on your drink as you would in Berlin or London, carry a copy or photo of your passport rather than the original, and keep your comanda and one bank card in separate pockets.

Frequently Asked Questions

What time do people actually go out in São Paulo?

Late. Dinner at 9 pm, bars from 10, samba concerts starting around midnight and clubs peaking at 2–3 am.

Bars start buzzing around 11 pm — this is not a city that rushes the night. Arriving at 9 pm at a club means drinking alone.

Do I need to speak Portuguese?

No, but learn three words: ‘uma comanda?’ (your tab card), ‘couvert’ (the music cover) and ‘a conta, por favor’ (the bill). Staff at Blue Note, Tokyo and the big clubs manage English; at the samba houses, smiling and pointing works perfectly.

Is tonight — a Thursday — actually a good night out?

One of the best. D-Edge’s Moving runs every Thursday, Villa Country opens Thursdays from 8 pm (with the Anime Friends Hotzone party tonight), Bar Brahma pours till 2 am and Tokyo runs till 5 am — Thursday is São Paulo’s unofficial first weekend night.

Rio de Janeiro · Nightlife

If You Only Go to One Place Samba na Fundição – Fundição Progresso, Lapa If you only do ONE thing tonight, make it Thursday’s samba at this vast old foundry under the Lapa Arches: every Thursday the Fundição Progresso hosts the great voices of carioca samba, from 9 pm to 4 am at Rua dos Arcos 24. The Samba Independente dos Bons Costumes roda plays every Thursday, the crowd is young, local and welcoming to foreigners, and when the roda ends you are already in the middle of Lapa’s street party.

Tonight at a Glance —Fundição Progresso (Samba na Fundição) Tonight’s big one – Thursday samba, 9 pm to 4 am, in Lapa; huge mixed local crowd, arrive by 10 pm —Beco do Rato The insiders’ roda – Thursdays at 9 pm the Encontros Casuais roda with Inácio Rios and Mosquito, famous for surprise guest sambistas; arrive 8 pm for a table —Bar Bip Bip 18 m² of pure music in Copacabana – Thursday samba from 9 pm; solo-friendly, all ages, magical and cheap —Rio Scenarium The beautiful three-floor antiques mansion on Rua do Lavradio – Thursdays everyone pays half price, tickets around R$20; great for dates and first-timers, doors 7 pm —Pink Flamingo Copacabana’s pop-queer bar-club near the Copacabana Palace – free entry bar vibe before 10 pm, then it turns into a party that runs till morning; open tonight

It is Thursday 2 July 2026 and Thursday is Rio’s secret best night: the weekend crowds have not landed, but every serious samba house is playing – the Samba na Fundição and the Encontros Casuais roda at Beco do Rato in Lapa, Bip Bip’s Thursday samba in Copacabana, plus half-price night at Rio Scenarium and a double jazz session at Blue Note. The classic circuit: sunset drink and early show around 7 pm, a roda de samba at 9 pm, Lapa’s streets after midnight, and a 99 or Uber home.

Tonight across Rio de Janeiro. (Photo internet reproduction)

What’s On Tonight

Samba na Fundição – weekly Thursday samba night (Samba Independente dos Bons Costumes roda) — at Fundição Progresso, Lapa, 9 pm (till 4 am). Every Thursday the Fundição hosts big names of carioca samba from 9 pm to 4 am – tonight’s definitive party, and 1 kg of food donated gets you 50% off entry

Encontros Casuais with Inácio Rios & Mosquito — at Beco do Rato, Lapa, 9 pm (bar from 6 pm). The traditional Thursday roda, with surprise guests and visiting sambistas – stars like Thiaguinho have dropped in unannounced

Thursday roda de samba — at Bar Bip Bip, Copacabana, 9 pm. The 1968 institution’s Thursday samba at 9 pm; you grab your own beer from the fridge and snap fingers instead of clapping – pure Rio

Half-price Thursday: live samba on the Palco Scenarium — at Rio Scenarium, Lapa/Centro, doors 7 pm, music from about 8 pm. Open Thursday 7 pm to 1 am and on Thursdays everyone pays half, around R$20 – the cheapest night at Rio’s most photogenic venue

Thursday samba show — at Carioca da Gema, Lapa, doors 7:30 pm, show 9 pm. Thursdays the house opens 7:30 pm with the show at 9 pm at the Lapa address that has presented the best of samba since 2000

Roda de samba in a 19th-century warehouse — at Trapiche Gamboa, Gamboa (Little Africa), doors 6:30 pm, roda 7:30-8:30 pm. Thursday doors at 6:30 pm, show from 7:30 pm – dance-floor samba in the neighbourhood where samba was born

Double session of jazz/MPB (two shows tonight) — at Blue Note Rio, Copacabana, free piano-bar happy hour from 5 pm; sessions 8 pm and 10:30 pm. Blue Note Rio has shows listed for 2 July 2026; Tuesday-Friday the house opens at 5 pm for a free happy hour, with the 8 pm session from 7 pm and a second session at 10 pm or 10:30 pm

Queer pop night with drag DJs — at Pink Flamingo, Copacabana, from 9 pm. Open every day from about 9 pm, with drag queens on the decks and a different musical style each night – tonight’s most reliable LGBTQ+ room

The Circuit: When to Go Where

Warm up 6:30-7:30 pm – Gamboa or Rua do Lavradio: doors open at Trapiche Gamboa and Rio Scenarium; eat, drink and catch the first set while it is calm

9 pm – the roda hour: commit to one Thursday samba – Fundição Progresso or Beco do Rato in Lapa, or Bip Bip if you are staying in Copacabana

Midnight – Lapa street mode: the streets around Avenida Mem de Sá and the Arches fill up; bar-hop between Carioca da Gema and the botecos

After 1 am – keep dancing: Fundição’s Thursday samba runs to 4 am; or slide to Pink Flamingo in Copacabana where the party goes till morning

Tomorrow and this weekend – Friday is Pedra do Sal’s free street samba (Mondays and Fridays from 6 pm) and Saturday 4 July is the 16th Arraiá do Circo with Geraldo Azevedo at Circo Voador

Scenes & Sounds

Samba — Rio’s heartbeat – live rodas where the crowd sings every word; Thursday is a proper samba night Where: Lapa (Fundição Progresso, Beco do Rato, Carioca da Gema), Gamboa (Trapiche Gamboa, Pedra do Sal), Copacabana (Bip Bip)

MPB — Brazilian popular music and gafieira ballroom dancing in grand old rooms Where: Rio Scenarium, with samba, gafieira, chorinho and pop across seven rooms of a 19th-century mansion

Choro & bossa nova — Instrumental virtuosity and the softest sound Rio ever made, in tiny botecos Where: Bip Bip – choro Tuesdays 8 pm, bossa nova Wednesdays 8 pm

Jazz & blues — Sit-down international-standard shows with dinner and cocktails by the beach Where: Blue Note Rio on Av. Atlântica in Copacabana – intimate jazz, MPB and instrumental shows with a sea view

Electronic — Underground and alternative club nights, indie upstairs and house/techno in the basement Where: Fosfobox in Copacabana – electronic, rock, pop and hip hop in a vanguard basement club; big roving parties announce on Instagram

Funk & Brazilian pop — Baile funk and pop bangers – mostly at weekend parties and queer nights rather than fixed clubs Where: Agyto and Portal near the Lapa Arches – young, diverse, Brazilian pop, funk and reggaeton, Fridays and Saturdays; Pink Flamingo for funk-pop tonight

Pick Your Night

Date night: Rio Scenarium – candlelit antiques, three floors, live samba and dancing; tonight it is also half price, so book a table and arrive 8 pm

Solo and safe: Bar Bip Bip, Copacabana – tiny, street-side, zero pretension; stand with the locals at tonight’s 9 pm samba, one beer at a time, and walk home along busy streets

Dance till sunrise: Fundição Progresso – tonight’s samba runs 9 pm to 4 am; on Fridays/Saturdays switch to Fosfobox’s basement till 6 am

Meet locals: Beco do Rato – a true carioca boteco roda where tables mix and everyone sings; go alone or in twos and you will leave with friends

Meet other expats: Blue Note Rio’s free 5 pm happy hour on the Copacabana beachfront, then Pink Flamingo – both draw an international, English-friendly crowd

Where to Go

Fundição Progresso — Lapa A former safe-and-stove factory turned huge independent cultural centre and Lapa’s most democratic dance floor; students, samba heads and gringos all mix here Tonight: Samba na Fundição – Thursday samba night, 9 pm to 4 am, with the resident SIBC roda Best time: Thursdays for samba, weekends for big-name shows; doors around 8-9 pm, arrive by 10 pm before the roda peaks Cost: Entry typically R$30-60 (half price if you bring 1 kg of food); beers ~R$10-15; card accepted, buy tickets on Sympla Address: Rua dos Arcos, 24 – Lapa Instagram: @fundicaoprogresso Website: www.fundicaoprogresso.com.br Getting there: Metro Cinelândia or Carioca then 10-min walk; rideshare drops at the door by the Arches Good to know: Buy online for big shows; tonight pay at door is usually fine; totally casual dress

Beco do Rato — Lapa Award-winning bar and samba house with rodas de samba every day; the crowd is carioca to the bone and the samba is roots, not show Tonight: Encontros Casuais at 9 pm, the traditional Thursday roda hosted by Inácio Rios and Mosquito Best time: Thursdays and Fridays; opens 6 pm, Thursdays until 1 am – arrive 8 pm to snag a table Cost: Roda nights from about R$25 entry, beers/caipirinhas cheap; card OK, advance tickets on Sympla Address: Rua Joaquim Silva, 11 – Lapa Phone: +55 21 2508-5600 Instagram: @becodorato WhatsApp: +55 21 97968-3670 Website: becodorato.com.br Getting there: Short walk from the Lapa Arches; rideshare to Rua Joaquim Silva Good to know: No dress code; buy the Sympla ticket ahead on busy weeks

Bar Bip Bip — Copacabana Founded in 1968 and just 18 m², yet one of the greatest places to hear music in Rio; musicians take the tables, punters spill onto the pavement Tonight: Thursday samba from 9 pm – a weekly certainty Best time: Sundays 7 pm and Thursdays 9 pm for samba; choro Tuesdays, bossa Wednesdays at 8 pm; arrive 8:30 pm – seats go fast Cost: No cover – drop money in the musicians’ tip jar; you fetch your own beer from the fridge and it goes on your tab; bring some cash Address: Rua Almirante Gonçalves, 50 – Copacabana Instagram: @rodadobip Getting there: Metro Cantagalo, 5-min walk; safe, busy corner of Copacabana Good to know: No bookings, no clapping – snap your fingers; be respectful of the neighbours

Rio Scenarium — Lapa / Rua do Lavradio (Centro) A 19th-century mansion with seven rooms, Brazilian food and live samba, gafieira, chorinho and pop – named one of the world’s 10 best bars by The Guardian; dressed-up locals, couples and visitors Tonight: Reliable Thursday standby: open 7 pm to 1 am with live samba on the main stage, and Thursdays at half price (~R$20) Best time: Thursday for value, Friday/Saturday for the full spectacle; arrive 8 pm to explore before the 8-9 pm first show Cost: ~R$20 Thursdays, more at weekends, plus food and drinks (cocktails ~R$25-40); cards accepted; official tickets via Sympla Address: Rua do Lavradio, 20 – Centro (Lapa) Phone: +55 21 3147-9000 Instagram: @rioscenarium Website: www.rioscenarium.com.br Getting there: Metro Carioca or Cinelândia then short walk; rideshare to the door on Rua do Lavradio Good to know: Book a table for dinner shows at weekends; smart-casual works, no beachwear

Carioca da Gema — Lapa Since 2000, one of the best places to live the carioca spirit, known for its exclusive samba programming; slightly older, music-loving crowd in an intimate two-storey casarão Tonight: Thursday: doors 7:30 pm, show at 9 pm – check @barcariocadagema for tonight’s artist Best time: Any night Tue-Sat; arrive for doors to get a table near the tiny stage Cost: Individual tickets from about R$25, tables from R$60 for two; couvert charged as entry; cards fine Address: Av. Mem de Sá, 79 – Lapa Phone: +55 21 98556-0834 Instagram: @barcariocadagema WhatsApp: +55 21 98556-0834 Website: www.barcariocadagema.com.br Getting there: Heart of Lapa’s main strip; metro Cinelândia + 8-min walk or rideshare Good to know: Book a table online for weekend nights; casual dress

Trapiche Gamboa — Gamboa / Little Africa A grand 19th-century sobrado in the cradle of samba, near the Pedra do Sal, built in 1867 with three floors; grown-up, dance-happy local crowd – people actually samba here Tonight: Thursday roda: house opens 6:30 pm, show from 7:30 pm Best time: Thursday-Saturday; come 7 pm for dinner, dance from 9 pm Cost: Entry/couvert up to about R$25; credit and debit cards accepted, and they take table reservations Address: Rua Sacadura Cabral, 155 – Gamboa Phone: +55 21 2516-0868 Getting there: Near Praça Mauá; VLT tram or rideshare door-to-door at night Good to know: Reserve a table by phone for Fri/Sat; weekend nights are 18+

Blue Note Rio — Copacabana The Rio branch of New York’s famous jazz club, an intimate room on Copacabana beach – polished, international, great for a classy night Tonight: Shows listed tonight, 2 July; free happy hour from 5 pm on the terrace and piano bar; 8 pm session with access from 7 pm, second session ~10:30 pm Best time: Tue-Sat; book the 8 pm session and come at 7 pm for dinner Cost: Happy hour free; show tickets vary by artist (roughly R$60-200 via Eventim); dinner and cocktails on top; cards everywhere Address: Av. Atlântica, 1910 – Copacabana Instagram: @bluenoterio Website: bluenoterio.com.br Getting there: Beachfront near Copacabana Palace; metro Cardeal Arcoverde + short walk, or rideshare Good to know: Yes – buy show tickets ahead; smart casual

Pink Flamingo — Copacabana A much-loved queer bar-club near the Copacabana Palace, known as Rio’s most pop LGBTQ+ spot with everyone from tourists to hipsters, bears and fashion kids Tonight: Open tonight – daily from about 9 pm, with drag queens DJing and a different style each night Best time: Every night, with Wednesday’s TRETA party as the weekly peak; arrive 10 pm for bar mode, midnight for the party Cost: Free before about 10 pm, paid entry later as it becomes a club; cocktails ~R$25-40; card OK Address: Rua Rodolfo Dantas, 16 – Copacabana Instagram: @pinkflamingorio Getting there: Metro Cardeal Arcoverde, 3-min walk; very central Copacabana Good to know: No booking; relaxed door, come as you are

Fosfobox — Copacabana A reference point for underground culture since 2004, with a varied roster of parties; a different party each day but always an alternative crowd – straight, gay, everything Tonight: Usually dark on Thursdays – core nights are Wednesday, Friday and Saturday, 11 pm to 6 am; keep it for tomorrow Best time: Fri/Sat from 11 pm; do not arrive before midnight Cost: Entry ~R$30-60 by party; you buy drink tickets and hand them to the bar, so no exit queue; drinks a bit pricey Address: Rua Siqueira Campos, 143 (loja 22A) – Copacabana Phone: +55 21 2548-7498 Website: fosfobox.com.br Getting there: Right by Siqueira Campos metro; night buses and rideshares outside Good to know: Names on the list via their socials can mean discounts; dress casual but stylish

Pedra do Sal (street samba) — Saúde / Little Africa Afro-Brazilian cultural heritage and symbol of black resistance in the Little Africa district – free open-air samba on historic stone steps; young, diverse, flip-flops-and-beer crowd Tonight: Not tonight – rodas are Mondays and Fridays from 6 pm, so pencil it for tomorrow evening Best time: Monday (the classic) and Friday, 6 pm till around midnight; go before 8 pm to get a spot on the rock Cost: Free; street vendors sell beer and caipirinhas for pocket change – bring cash and Pix if you have it Address: Rua Argemiro Bulcão / Largo João da Baiana – Saúde Instagram: @pedradosaloficial Getting there: Nearest metros are Uruguaiana and Carioca – Carioca is farther but the nicer walk; rideshare straight there after dark Good to know: No booking – it is a street party; keep phones tucked away in the crowd

Neighbourhoods at a Glance

Lapa: Rio’s bohemian engine room – samba houses, mega-venues and street drinking under the Arches; young, loud, everyone from everywhere

Centro / Rua do Lavradio: Antique-shop street that turns elegant at night around Rio Scenarium; a dressier, date-friendly slice of old Rio

Gamboa / Little Africa (Saúde): The old port area known as Little Africa – the birthplace of samba; soulful rodas, historic warehouses, go by rideshare at night

Copacabana: Crowded, rowdy and traditional, with a bit of everything – music bars, pubs and chaotic streets plus jazz at Blue Note and queer nights near the Palace

Ipanema / Leblon: Chic beach-adjacent bars, cocktails and the LGBTQ+ strip around Rua Teixeira de Melo; polished crowd, earlier nights

Botafogo: The local hipster quarter – craft beer, indie bars and queer-friendly lounges like Vuvu; where young cariocas drink midweek

LGBTQ+ Tonight

Pink Flamingo (Copacabana) — Rio’s most pop gay bar-balada: free pub mode before 10 pm, full party till morning after – open TONIGHT, drag DJs, every flavour of crowd

La Cueva (Copacabana) — One of Rio’s most traditional LGBTQ+ clubs, going for over six decades, cave-like and intimate, drawing mature men and bears; open Thursday to Sunday from 10 pm – an option tonight

Galeria Café (Ipanema) — A rotating home of queer parties – drag contests, bear nights, Madonna nights, samba nights; open Thursday to Sunday with a pop, tourist-friendly floor

Money & How Paying Works The comanda: at most bars and clubs you get a paper or plastic tab card at the door; every drink is marked on it and you pay everything at the till on the way OUT – guard it, because losing it means paying a hefty fixed fine. (You will queue to pay before you can leave – Fosfobox flips this with pre-paid drink tickets you hand to the bar, avoiding the exit queue.) Couvert artístico: live-music venues add a music cover per person (roughly R$15-60) either at the door or on your bill – it pays the band, it is normal, and Thursday deals exist (Rio Scenarium charges half, about R$20, on Thursdays). Cards are accepted almost everywhere (even traditional samba houses take credit and debit), but carry R$50-100 in small notes for street vendors, Pedra do Sal-style rodas and tips; locals also pay by Pix, which you cannot use without a Brazilian account. Tipping: 10% service (‘serviço’) is usually already on the bill – just check the receipt; if it is not there, adding 10% is the norm, and tip jars at free rodas like Bip Bip keep the music alive.

Getting Home Safe

MetrôRio runs until around midnight on weekdays, so tonight assume the last train leaves before you do – fine for an early Blue Note or Bip Bip night, useless after a 2 am samba.

Use 99 or Uber, not street taxis: order from inside the venue or a bright doorway (Fundição’s entrance, Rio Scenarium’s door on Lavradio, the Copacabana Palace corner for Pink Flamingo), confirm the plate before getting in, and share your trip in the app.

Expect surge pricing when Lapa empties out between 3 and 4 am – either leave at 2:30 am or have one last beer and wait ten minutes for prices to settle; split fares with new friends heading the same way along the Zona Sul.

Lapa and the samba districts are festive and well-policed but pickpockets work the crowds: take one card and modest cash, keep your phone in a front pocket, only pull it out with your back to a wall, and leave the passport and watch at home.

Stick to the lit, busy streets – Mem de Sá, the Arches, Rua do Lavradio – and move between neighbourhoods by rideshare rather than on foot after midnight; if you are ever hassled, hand over the phone without argument and replace it, not your night.

Frequently Asked Questions

What time do people actually go out in Rio?

Late, but Thursday samba is merciful: doors 6:30-7:30 pm, rodas at 9 pm, peak 11 pm-1 am. Clubs like Fosfobox are empty before midnight; nobody blinks if you arrive at a party at 1 am.

Do I need to book anything for tonight?

Mostly no – pay at the door at Fundição, Beco do Rato and Bip Bip. Book ahead for Blue Note Rio shows and for a table at Rio Scenarium or Carioca da Gema at weekends; Brazilian venues sell via Sympla/Eventim and answer fastest on Instagram DMs or WhatsApp.

I don’t speak Portuguese – will I cope?

Yes. Point at the menu, learn ‘uma cerveja, por favor’ and ‘a conta’ (the bill), and remember the comanda card is your tab. In Lapa and Copacabana staff are used to foreigners, and a smile plus attempted Portuguese buys enormous goodwill.

World.title: Guinea’s Simandou Ships Its First Iron Ore to China
World.content:
By subscribing you agree to our privacy policy . We never share your email.

The morning intel from across Latin America. Free.

GUINEA · MARKETS

Key Facts —First shipment: The bulk carrier Winning Youth left Guinea on 2 December 2025, and the first ore reached China in January 2026. —The owners: Two ventures run the mine: Simfer, led by Rio Tinto with China’s Chinalco, and the Chinese-dominated Winning Consortium Simandou. —This year’s output: Simfer expects 5 to 10 million tonnes in 2026; exports reached about 2.2 million tonnes in May, up from 1.3 million in April. —Full capacity: The project is ramping up over roughly 30 months toward 60 million tonnes a year, and as much as 120 million eventually. —The scale: The IMF says Simandou could become the largest iron mine on Earth. —The strategy: For China, the mine loosens a long reliance on iron ore from Australia.

Simandou iron ore has started leaving Guinea for China, opening one of the largest mining projects on Earth and giving Beijing a fresh source of the raw material its steel mills depend on.

What Simandou iron ore is and why it matters

Simandou is a vast, high-grade iron ore deposit in the mountains of southeastern Guinea. It has been called the world’s largest untapped reserve of the metal.

For decades it sat idle, tangled in disputes and the sheer cost of building mines, a railway and a port from scratch.

Rival companies fought for years over the rights, and one earlier deal collapsed in a corruption scandal that reached the courts.

Building the mine also meant carving a roughly 600-kilometre railway through jungle and mountains to a brand-new port.

Now the ore is finally moving, and it could reshape the global market for the raw material that steel is made from.

Iron ore is the single most important ingredient in steel, and steel underpins everything from bridges and buildings to cars and machines.

China alone produces more than half the world’s steel, so its appetite for ore shapes the entire global market.

How the mine is owned

The project is split between two ventures. Simfer is led by the Anglo-Australian giant Rio Tinto alongside China’s state-owned Chinalco.

The other half, the Winning Consortium Simandou, is dominated by Chinese interests, including the steel giant China Baowu, with Singaporean investors involved.

That structure gives China deep influence over a mine on the other side of the world.

The two ventures share the mine, the railway and the port, an arrangement that took years of hard bargaining to settle.

Rio Tinto brings the mining know-how, while its Chinese partners bring the capital and a guaranteed buyer for the ore.

The ramp-up

The first commercial cargo left Guinea in December 2025 and reached China early in 2026. Volumes are climbing fast.

Exports hit about 2.2 million tonnes in May, up from 1.3 million in April, according to shipment data.

Simfer expects 5 to 10 million tonnes this year, building over about 30 months toward 60 million tonnes annually, and up to 120 million in time.

Why China wanted it

China makes more than half the world’s steel and has long depended on Australia and Brazil for its iron ore. That reliance is a strategic weak spot.

Simandou gives Chinese mills a large new supply they part-own and can count on. It is a hedge against tension with Canberra.

The IMF says the mine could eventually rival the biggest in the world, enough to move global prices.

A surge of new supply could push iron ore prices lower, reshaping the fortunes of established miners from Australia to Brazil.

What it means for Guinea

For Guinea, one of the world’s poorest countries, Simandou is a once-in-a-generation chance. The state holds a stake and stands to earn royalties and taxes.

The build also delivered a roughly 600-kilometre railway and a new port, infrastructure the country never had.

The risk is that the windfall is mismanaged or that the environmental cost, in a fragile mountain region, outweighs the gains.

Guinea has cycled through coups and contested governments, and critics fear the money could vanish into weak institutions.

Handled well, though, the revenue could pay for schools, clinics and power in one of West Africa’s poorest states.

The bigger scramble

Simandou is a vivid piece of a wider contest for Africa’s resources. Great powers are racing to lock up the minerals that modern economies run on.

China’s grip on the project sits alongside Western efforts to secure critical minerals elsewhere on the continent.

How Guinea manages its new wealth will shape whether Simandou becomes a model or a cautionary tale.

For now the ore is moving, and a project long dismissed as impossible has finally begun to deliver.

The next test is whether the benefits reach ordinary Guineans rather than a well-connected few.

World.title: Fonseca and Arévalo Keep Latin America Alive at Wimbledon
World.content:
Latin America’s Wimbledon picture has narrowed quickly, leaving Brazil’s João Fonseca as the region’s clearest singles contender and El Salvador’s Marcelo Arévalo as Central America’s strongest remaining title threat.

Fonseca, the No. 24 seed, moved into the third round after beating Roberto Bautista Agut in his opener and Jesper de Jong in straight sets. He now faces Roman Safiullin, a grass-court test that could determine whether the Brazilian teenager becomes one of the tournament’s breakout second-week stories.

After opening Wimbledon as one of Latin America’s top names, Fonseca has now become the region’s leading men’s singles survivor. That gives this run a different weight from a normal early-round result. Latin American tennis often builds its biggest Grand Slam hopes on clay, but Fonseca’s power, serve and calm under pressure have translated well to grass.

For us here in Costa Rica and across Central America, the strongest regional connection remains Arévalo. The Salvadoran doubles standout and Croatian partner Mate Pavić, seeded sixth, beat Alexander Bublik and Nick Kyrgios 6-3, 6-4 in the first round of men’s doubles.

That win keeps a Central American player alive at one of the sport’s biggest events. Arévalo has already built one of the most successful careers ever by a player from this region, and his presence gives Wimbledon a local thread even without a Costa Rican player in the main singles draw. The broader Latin American singles field has taken hits.

Peru’s Ignacio Buse won his opening match before falling to Jenson Brooksby in the second round. Colombia’s Nicolás Mejía also won once, beating Paraguay’s Adolfo Daniel Vallejo before losing to Michael Zheng. Chile’s Alejandro Tabilo went out in the first round against Kamil Majchrzak, while Argentina’s Francisco Cerúndolo, one of the region’s higher-seeded men, lost his opener to Jaume Munar.

Argentina still had one of the most dramatic moments of the early rounds through Solana Sierra, who pushed Coco Gauff deep into a deciding tiebreak before losing in three sets. Sierra led late in the breaker before Gauff won the final stretch, turning a possible upset into a narrow escape for one of the tournament’s biggest names.

On the women’s side, Colombia’s Camila Osorio gave Latin America another early win, beating Simona Waltert 6-2, 6-1. Her next challenge was a much tougher one against No. 9 seed Linda Noskova. Other regional names had shorter stays, including Brazil’s Beatriz Haddad Maia, Mexico’s Renata Zarazúa and Argentina’s Nadia Podoroska.

The pattern is familiar. Wimbledon gives Latin American players less time to settle than clay or hard courts. Grass rewards quick points, low movement, first serves and clean returns. Players who build through longer rallies often have to adjust fast or leave early.
